description:
We are Moon-jigi, two close friends studying together at KAIST.

Our name is a Korean wordplay. "Moonjigi (문지기)" means gatekeeper in Korean, and "moon (문)" means gate. So we are the keepers of the Moon's gate. Our project does just that: it scores landing sites at the lunar south pole and decides which ones are ready to let a mission through.

We love technology, science, and solving real-world problems from an engineering perspective, and we're excited to bring that curiosity to the NASA Space Apps Challenge!
summary: At the Moon's south pole the Sun stays close to the horizon, so nearby hills often block it. Landing a few days late or a few hundred metres off target can leave a lander without power or without a radio link to Earth. Moon-jigi (Korean for "gatekeeper") is a web tool for one practical question: if we land here on this date and stay 6 or 14 days, will we have enough sunlight and Earth contact? You pick a site and a date and get GO or NO-GO. If the answer is NO-GO, the tool shows which ridge is in the way and suggests the smallest change that works: land nearby or wait a few days. If your lander carries its antenna and panels on a mast, it also tells you how tall that mast would need to be. If you have no site yet, you can scan the whole south pole for ground that passes. Everything uses NASA LOLA terrain and is shown in 3D, with the Sun and Earth moving across the sky. We built it for mission planners choosing south-pole landing sites and dates (including re-planning after a launch slip), small lander teams that cannot run their own lighting study, and classrooms learning why the Sun barely rises at the pole.
details:
1. WHAT WE FOUND
We checked every landing day of 2027 at 12 sites: one in each of NASA’s nine Artemis III regions, plus three more. For a 6-day stay with default limits, 67.0% of landing days are NO-GO without a mast (75.5% for a 14-day stay). For 39.1% of them, a GO day comes within the next 7 days (69.2% within 14 days). For 7.3%, a passing spot lies within 1 km. For a lander that carries its panels and antenna on a mast of 20 m or less, 11.0% would pass at the same spot and date.

2. HOW IT WORKS
A landing site gets a GO if, over the whole stay of 6 or 14 days, it meets all three conditions:

  • Sunlight: at least 90% of the time
  • Earth visibility: Earth above the horizon at least 50% of the time
  • Longest darkness: no unbroken dark spell longer than 50 hours

Why these defaults (users can adjust all three): Sunlight 90%, because solar-powered landers such as CLPS expect sunlight for the whole stay, so we allow only a 10% margin. Darkness 50 hours, the longest dark spell NASA planned for the VIPER rover to survive on battery. Earth 50%, because a south-pole lander is expected to rely on direct-to-Earth radio (NASA lunar site selection review), so Earth must be in view. The 50% value itself is our own assumption (Earth in view for at least half the stay), not a published requirement. A percentage can hide long gaps: in our 2027 runs (6-day stay), 11.3% of GO days still lose Earth for more than 50 hours in a row. A limit on the longest continuous Earth blackout could replace the percentage, but how many hours to allow is still an open question (with 50 hours, GO days would drop from 1,444 to 1,281).

Why 6 and 14 days: 6 days is the planned surface stay of Artemis III (George et al., LPSC 2026). 14 days is one lunar daytime, the period a solar-powered CLPS lander is designed to work through.

We computed the Sun and Earth positions for every hour of 2027 (8,760 hours) using JPL ephemerides and the IAU lunar rotation model, including Earth’s libration in the lunar sky. Each position is checked against the real terrain horizon from NASA LOLA data.

Landers with a mast: we do not design landers or prescribe hardware, so a mast is not one of our fixes. If your lander carries its solar panels and antenna on a mast, the tool also reports the lowest mast height that clears the ridge. Up to 20 m (the default maximum, which users can change) the site is shown as "GO with N m mast", and 15 m or more is flagged HIGH.

3. FEATURES

1) CHECK a landing
Pick a site, a landing date and a stay, and get GO or NO-GO in one sentence. There are 12 reference sites: one point in each of NASA’s nine Artemis III candidate regions (2024), plus Shackleton Rim, the Connecting Ridge and the IM-2 landing target. The screen shows why:

  • 3D terrain with the blocking ridge drawn in red
  • Sun and Earth direction arrows
  • Sky plot of the Sun’s and Earth’s paths over the real horizon
  • Calendar of every GO day in 2027

2) FIX a NO-GO
Moon-jigi looks for the smallest change in where or when to land:

  • MOVE: the nearest passing location within 3 km (landing slope 8° or less), shown on the map
  • WAIT: the next landing date that meets all three conditions

3) FIND a new site
No candidate yet? Combine map layers for sunlight, Earth visibility, darkness duration, terrain slope and water-ice stability grade (at the surface, within 0.5 m, 0.5–1 m, or none) from LRO Diviner temperatures. For a chosen date, the tool ranks the five best spots, and you can compare a shortlist side by side on the same landing date.

Also: the /api/check endpoint returns the same GO/NO-GO answer as JSON, so other applications can use it.

4. VALIDATION

  • Accuracy: our sunlight and Earth-visibility maps agree with NASA reference maps to within 2.3 and 2.7 percentage points.
  • Consistency: we ran 36,160 automated checks to confirm that the website and the API give the same answers.
  • Robustness: we re-checked every GO verdict of 2027 (6-day stay, 4,950 GO results) two ways. On the next coarser terrain model, 98.8% stay GO, and every type stays above 96%. When the lander touches down 30 m off target (8 directions), 83.7% stay GO: 93.9% of days that are GO as planned, 81.2% after WAIT, 80.9% after MOVE and 63.2% with a mast, because many mast heights clear the ridge only just.
  • Past missions: we checked real south-pole landings and impacts on their actual dates. IM-2 Athena (March 6, 2025) is GO at its target (Sun 94%, Earth 89%). Its tip-over in a small crater happened at a scale finer than our 20 m terrain grid. The LCROSS, Lunar Prospector and Chandrayaan-1 impact sites are NO-GO, as expected for permanently shadowed ground. All of them are shown on the map.

5. WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE
Existing lunar lighting tools tell you how much sunlight a location gets. We wanted ours to also say what to do when a site fails: where and when to land instead.

  • Where to land (location)
  • When to land (date)

Each suggestion is a distance in metres or a number of days.

6. FACTORS WE CONSIDERED
At the south pole the Sun stays low, so nearby hills and crater rims block it for long periods. Our model includes:

  • Horizon blocking: uses the real surrounding terrain, not flat-ground sunlight
  • Earth libration: Earth’s changing position in the lunar sky
  • Battery survival: checks the longest dark spell, which a lander’s battery must outlast
  • Landing slope: site points are limited to slopes of 8° or less
  • Water ice: how deep ice could stay frozen, from LRO Diviner temperatures (the same idea NASA used to plan VIPER)

Note: the 12 sites are worked examples we picked in advance. In each region we combined the data above and chose a point that does well on average (sunlight, Earth view, gentle slope). They give students and planners a ready starting point.

Next step: KPLO ShadowCam (NASA/KARI) images can see inside permanently shadowed craters. They could be used to check our ice-stability grade against the real surface.

7. TOOLS & TECHNOLOGY

  • Data pipeline: Python
  • Web app and 3D views: JavaScript, WebGL
  • Hosting and API: Cloudflare Pages and Pages Functions
